'''''Tragopogon dubius''''', commonly known as '''yellow salsify''', is a species of [[Tragopogon|salsify]] with yellow flower heads. It is native to Eurasia and has been introduced to North America.

== Description ==
Like most salsifies, ''Tragopogon dubius'' grows as an [[annual plant|annual]] or occasionally [[biennial plant|biennial]] [[forb]],{{Citation needed|date=April 2025}} reaching a height of {{Convert|40–80|cm|frac=2}}. The [[leaves]] are up to {{Convert|25|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} long.<ref name="auduflo">{{Cite book |last=Spellenberg |first=Richard |url=https://archive.org/details/nationalaudubons00spel/page/402/ |title=National Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers: Western Region |publisher=Knopf |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-375-40233-3 |edition=rev |pages=403 |orig-date=1979}}</ref>

The buds are blue-green, tall, and tapered. On display from late spring to late summer, the yellow [[flower head]] is {{Convert|4–5|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} wide.<ref name="auduflo" /> The inflorescence opens early in the morning and often closes up by late afternoon. Later, the plant forms a seed head resembling that of [[dandelion]]s, but distinctly larger.

The seeds (known as [[achene]]s) are 2–4 cm long but featherweight, weighing about 8 mg each on average. There is some natural variation between the central and peripheral achenes in the [[seedhead]], with the peripheral ones being generally darker and heavier, and having a higher concentration of [[phenol]]ic compounds; this may enhance their survival potential.

=== Similar species ===
[[File:Tragopogon dubius seedhead.jpg|thumb|''T. dubius'', large seedhead]]

Similar species include the widespread [[Tragopogon pratensis|''T. pratensis'']] (meadow salsify), the [[bract]]s of which are shorter than the rays.<ref name="auduflo" />

== Taxonomy ==
Although not particularly closely related to [[Tragopogon porrifolius|''T. porrifolius'']] or ''T. pratensis'', ''T. dubius'' [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridises]] readily with both, and in North America its hybrids have given rise to the new [[alloploidy|alloploid]] hybrid species [[Tragopogon mirus|''T. mirus'']] and [[Tragopogon miscellus|''T. miscellus'']].

=== Names ===
It has a [[synonym (biology)|synonym]], ''Tragopogon major''.

Its [[common name]]s include yellow salsify,<ref>{{PLANTS|id=TRDU|taxon=Tragopogon dubius|accessdate=14 December 2015}}</ref> western salsify, western goat's-beard, wild oysterplant, yellow goat's beard, meadow goat's beard, goat's beard (or goatsbeard), common salsify, and salsify. Some of these are also, perhaps more commonly, used for other species.{{Citation needed|date=April 2025}}

== Distribution and habitat ==
It is native to [[Southern Europe|southern]] and [[central Europe]] and [[western Asia]] and found as far north and west as northern [[France]]. Although it has been reported from [[Kashmir]] and [[India]], recent evidence{{citation needed|date=February 2022}} suggests that specimens from these areas may be a different species.

It has been [[introduced species|introduced]] into North America<ref name="auduflo" /> where it has become widespread, being reported from all the [[continental United States]] except for a few in the far southeast, and all [[provinces of Canada]] except Newfoundland and the northern territories.

It grows typically in fields and [[disturbed area]]s.<ref name="auduflo" />

== Uses ==
The edibility of wild western salsify is disputed. In ''The Medicinal and Poisonous Plants of Southern and Eastern Africa'' (1962) by Watt and Breyer-Brandwijk it is reported to be inedible. However, Stephen Facciola wrote in his book ''Cornucopia'' (1990) that the flowering stems, buds, leaves, shoots, and roots are all edible.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Duke |first1=James A. |author1-link=James A. Duke |title=Handbook of Edible Weeds |date=1992 |publisher=CRC Press |location=Boca Raton, Florida |isbn=978-0-8493-4225-7 |page=196}}</ref>

Though [[purple salsify]] (''Tragopogon porrifolus'') is also called oyster root, both western salsify and [[meadow salsify]] (''Tragopogon pratensis'') have roots that are much more strongly flavored, but that are both fibrous and bitter. Garden grown roots of all species are more easily eaten than wild harvested roots.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Tilford |first1=Gregory L. |title=Edible and Medicinal Plants of the West |date=1997 |publisher=Mountain Press Publishing |location=Missoula, Montana |isbn=978-0-87842-359-0 |page=132}}</ref>

The edibility of '''yellow salsify''' as discussed above referencing James Duke's book may have used information on '''purple salsify'''.
Referencing Watt and Breyer-Brandwijk's book on the Internet Archives, they do not refer to the YELLOW variety, but to 
''Tragopogon porrifolius L.'' the cultivated PURPLE salsify which grows as an escape in some parts of South Africa. The cultivated root is edible but the wild variety is inedible. From Australia it is reported that the young wild plant is eaten by cattle but not when it is in flower. In Europe the root has been used as an aperitif and as an expectorant and the stalk as a vegetable. In the United States of America the plant has been found to contain about 0-1 per cent of rubber.

Referencing Facciola's book on the Internet Archives they do not refer to the YELLOW variety, but to the PURPLE
''Tragopogon porrifolius L.''. Salsify, Oyster plant, Vegetable oyster. Roots are eaten raw in salads, boiled, baked, sauteed in butter, added to soups, or grated and made into cakes. The young shoots (chards), flower buds, and flowers may be eaten in salads, either raw or cooked and cooled. Flowers are also pickled. Young flower-stalks are cooked and dressed like asparagus. Sprouted seeds can be used in salads and sandwiches. The milky latex from the roots was used as chewing gum by British Columbia Indians.

Neither Watt and Breyer-Brandwijk nor Facciola discuss ''Tragopogon dubius''.
